Franchise Item 19 Reality Check

How to read a franchise Item 19 earnings claim

Item 19 is where a franchisor may tell you what its units earn. It is the most useful page in the document and the easiest to misread. Four checks take ten minutes.

1. How many units are in the table?

Compare the number of units in the table with the number in the system (Item 20 lists it). Franchisors often leave out units open less than a year, closed units and company-owned units. If the table covers half the system, ask what happened to the other half.

2. Average or median?

The average adds everything up; the median is the middle unit. In the worked example below four equal-sized quartiles report 1,450,000, 1,020,000, 810,000 and 560,000 of annual revenue. The average is 960,000, but the middle unit earns 810,000, and half the units are below the average.

3. Convert sales to owner earnings

Assume royalty 6%, ad fund 2%, cost of goods 30%, other variable costs 3%, and fixed costs of 180,000 a year. That is 41% of revenue in variable costs. At 810,000 of revenue, variable costs are 332,100 and owner earnings are 810,000 − 332,100 − 180,000 = 297,900. At 560,000, they are 560,000 − 229,600 − 180,000 = 150,400.

4. Payback and your own pay

With a 350,000 investment, 297,900 of owner earnings pays back in about 1.2 years before tax, debt service and ramp-up; 150,400 takes about 2.3 years. If you need 70,000 a year to live on, subtract it first. Use the reality check to run your own numbers.

Common questions

Is a high average in Item 19 a good sign?

Only if most units are near it. An average that sits far above the median means a few large units are lifting the number. Look at the quartile table and the share of units below the average before you read anything into the headline.

Does Item 19 tell me what I will earn?

No. It describes what other units earned in a past period, under the franchisor's definitions. Your sales depend on your location, your ramp-up and your own management, and your owner earnings depend on costs the table usually omits.

Who should I ask if the numbers look too good?

Franchisees listed in Item 20, including those who recently left, and an independent franchise attorney and accountant. A franchisor's own broker is paid when you sign.

FRANCHISE ITEM 19 REALITY CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What does that franchise earnings claim mean for you?

Type in the tiers from Item 19 of a franchise disclosure document. The page shows the average against the median, how much of the system the figures cover, what each tier keeps after royalty, ad fund and your own costs, the payback on your investment, and the share of units that would not pay you a salary.

For people weighing a franchise purchase. New to the document? Read how to read an Item 19 earnings claim, with a worked example.

1. Item 19 tiers

2. Your costs and investment

Item 7 of the document lists the investment range; Items 5 and 6 list the fees. Item 19 sales figures usually exclude all of this, and some include or exclude owner labor, so read its footnotes.

Enter the tiers, then click Check the claim.

TierUnitsRevenueRoyalty + ad fundOwner earningsAfter your salaryPayback

Sales you would need

How it works

Average and median: the average is total reported revenue over reporting units. The median is the tier containing the middle unit. When the average is well above the median, a few strong units are lifting the headline number.

Coverage: if you enter the number of units in the system, the page shows what share the figures describe. You can assume the missing units earn a fraction of the reported average to see the system-wide figure that implies. That fraction is your assumption.

Owner earnings: revenue minus the percentage costs (royalty, ad fund, cost of goods, scaling labor, other) minus fixed costs. Payback is investment divided by owner earnings, before tax, debt service and any ramp-up period.

Not modelled: a first-year ramp, loan payments, taxes, working capital, renewal and transfer fees, required remodels, and whether the document's figures include owner labor. Read the footnotes to Item 19 and talk to current and former franchisees listed in Item 20.

Related tool: the franchise unit economics calculator builds a month-by-month cash plan from your own assumptions.

Checked: the test suite recomputes hand-worked cases for owner earnings, break-even, payback and the coverage adjustment.

Common questions

What is Item 19 in a franchise disclosure document?

Item 19 is the section of the Franchise Disclosure Document where a franchisor may state what its franchised or company units earn, such as average sales, quartiles or profit. It is optional, so many franchisors say nothing, and the figures usually cover only some units over some period, with footnotes that define which ones.

How do I read Item 19 figures without being misled?

Start with how many units the figures cover compared with the whole system, then compare the average with the median. A high average over a small share of units, or an average far above the median, describes the best operators rather than a typical new buyer. This page shows both, and what each tier earns after royalty, ad fund and your own costs.

Are Item 19 sales figures the same as profit?

No. Most Item 19 tables report gross sales or revenue. Royalty, ad fund, cost of goods, labor, rent and your own pay all come out of that figure, so two units with the same sales can have very different owner earnings. Enter your own cost assumptions and the page converts each tier from sales to owner earnings.

What if only some units are included in Item 19?

Franchisors often exclude new units, closed units, company-owned units or units that were not open a full year. If the figures cover well under the whole system, the page lets you assume the missing units earn a share of the reported average and shows the system-wide figure that implies. That share is your assumption, not a fact from the document.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. Everything is calculated in your browser, nothing is sent to a server, and there are no accounts.
